entities.summary:
The 2015–16 Zika virus epidemic was a major public health crisis that took place in Brazil, starting on April 1, 2015, and ending on November 1, 2016.

This epidemic was caused by the rapid spread of the Zika virus, which was primarily transmitted through the bite of infected mosquitoes. The virus was first detected in Brazil in May 2015 and quickly spread to other parts of the country, as well as to neighboring countries in South America.

The Zika virus epidemic had significant consequences for public health, particularly for pregnant women and their unborn children. The virus was linked to a surge in cases of microcephaly, a rare birth defect in which the baby's head is significantly smaller than normal. This led to a significant increase in the number of babies born with microcephaly, as well as other birth defects.

The epidemic also had significant economic and social consequences, particularly in Brazil, which was hosting the 2016 Summer Olympics. The epidemic forced the cancellation of several events, and led to a significant increase in the number of people seeking medical care.

As the epidemic came to an end, it left a lasting legacy in the world of public health. The crisis highlighted the need for improved surveillance and response systems for infectious diseases, as well as the importance of international cooperation in addressing global health crises.

The Zika virus epidemic will be remembered as a major public health crisis that had significant consequences for the people of Brazil and beyond.

The World Health Organization (WHO) reported that there were over 200,000 cases of Zika virus reported in the Americas during 2015 and 2016, with over 2,400 cases of microcephaly reported in Brazil alone.
